bio: Al-Mizzi's Tahdhib al-Kamal (islamweb edition) names him Muhammad ibn Dinar al-Azdi then al-Tahi, Abu Bakr al-Basri. The page reports mixed gradings: some called him truthful (saduq), others weak, and he is said to have deteriorated before his death. Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrate from him. No death year is given.

He narrated from Hawshab, a companion of al-Hasan al-Basri, and Musa ibn Isma'il narrated from him. Ibn Hibban listed him in al-Thiqat. No death year is given.

He narrated from Ghalib al-Tammar and al-Nahhas ibn Qahm, and transmitted a report on the virtue of fasting in the first ten days. Ibn Hibban listed him in al-Thiqat. No death year is given.

He narrates in Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, and the entry quotes al-Khatib calling him 'a truthful shaykh' (shaykh saduq). No death year is given.

bio: Al-Mizzi's Tahdhib al-Kamal names him Yusuf ibn Khalid ibn 'Umayr al-Samti, Abu Khalid al-Basri, father of Khalid ibn Yusuf al-Samti. It quotes Yahya ibn Ma'in calling him weak and a bad man from whom no good narrator transmits. It quotes Abu Musa Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna that he died in 189 AH (continuation page https://shamela.ws/book/3722/17539).

full: Sa'd ibn ar-Rabi' bin 'Amr bin Abi Zuhair b. Malik b. Imru'ul-Qays b. Malik b. Tha'laba b. Ka'b
full_name_ar: سعد بن الربيع بن عمرو بن أبي زهير ( رضي الله عنه
bio: The page says he was an Ansari companion of the Khazraj, one of the chiefs (nuqaba) at the Second Pledge of al-Aqaba, and that the Prophet made him a brother of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. He fought at Badr and was killed at Uhud in 3 AH. The page cites Ibn Sa'd's al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Ibn al-Athir's Usd al-Ghaba, al-Dhahabi's Siyar A'lam al-Nubala and Ibn Hajar's al-Isaba.
research_evidence: سعد بن الربيع (المتوفي سنة 3 هـ) صحابي من بني كعب بن الخزرج بن الحارث بن الخزرج

full: Liala Bint Abi Hathmah b. Hudhafa b. Ghanm b. 'Amir b. 'Abdullah b. 'Ubaid b. 'Uwaij b. 'Adi b. Ka'b

bio: The page says she was a Qurashi woman of Banu 'Adi, wife of 'Amir ibn Rabi'a and mother of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir, and one of the women on the first migration to Abyssinia. It reports she may have been the first woman to arrive in Medina as an emigrant, and that she transmitted hadith. The page cites al-Tabarani's al-Mu'jam al-Kabir, Ibn al-Athir's Usd al-Ghaba, al-Hakim's al-Mustadrak and Ibn Sa'd's al-Tabaqat al-Kubra.
research_evidence: ليلى بنت أبي حثمة القرشية العدوية، أخت سليمان بن أبي حثمة، وأم عبد الله بن عامر بن ربيعة

famous: Ruqayqa bint Abi Sayfi bin Hashim

full_name_ar: رقيقة بنت أبي صيفي بن هاشم ( رضي الله عنها
bio: Ibn Hajar's al-Isaba (entry 11182) gives her as Ruqayqa bint Abi Sayfi ibn Hashim al-Hashimiyya, mother of Makhrama. He says al-Tabarani and al-Mustaghfiri listed her among the Companions, while Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) doubted that she met the Prophet. She is the narrator of the report about Abd al-Muttalib's prayer for rain, which she witnessed, and verses beginning 'بشيبة الحمد أسقى اللَّه بلدتنا' are attributed to her.

full: Najiyah or 'Atika or Fakhta bint al-Walid b. al-Mughirah b. 'Abdullah b. 'Umar b. Makhzum

She became Muslim on the day of the conquest of Mecca and gave the pledge; Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) says she converted a month before her husband. Ibn Manda says she is mentioned but has no hadith.

full: Qaraybah bint Abi Umayyah b. al-Mughirah b. 'Abdullah b. 'Umar b. Makhzum b. Yaqazah b. Murrah
full_name_ar: قريبة بنت أبي أمية ( رضي الله عنها

It quotes al-Baladhuri that Mu'awiya married her when he became Muslim, and reports that Abd al-Rahman (son of Abu Bakr) married her and she refused to choose anyone over 'the son of al-Siddiq'. It also cites Umar ibn Shabba's Kitab Makka that she was known for her beauty.

full: Umm Hakim bint al-Harith ibn Hisham b. al-Mughirah b. 'Abdullah b. 'Umar b. Makhzum
full_name_ar: أم حكيم بنت الحارث بن هشام بن المغيرة ( رضي الله عنها
bio: Wikipedia says she was the daughter of al-Harith ibn Hisham of Banu Makhzum and Fatima bint al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. She converted at the conquest of Mecca in 630 and persuaded her husband Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl to convert; she later married Khalid ibn Sa'id and then Umar ibn al-Khattab, bearing him Fatima. At the Battle of Marj al-Saffar (634) she is reported to have killed seven Byzantine soldiers with a tent pole. The page cites al-Waqidi, al-Baladhuri and al-Tabari.
research_evidence: Umm Ḥakīm bint al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām (Arabic: أم حكيم بنت الحارث إبن هشام) was a female disciple (known in Arabic as Sahaba or companions) of Islamic prophet Muhammad.
dod_s: c. 680 CE (estimated from generation — no recorded date survives)

full: Bukayr/Bakr bin Shaddakh al-Laithi
full_name_ar: بكير - بكر بن الشداخ الليثي ( رضي الله عنه
bio: Ibn Hajar's al-Isaba (entry 728) gives him as Bakr ibn al-Shaddakh al-Laythi, also called Bukayr. Ibn Manda reports that he served the Prophet as a boy and, on reaching puberty, told the Prophet, who prayed for him. Hisham ibn al-Kalbi (Kitab al-Nasab) and Sayf ibn Umar (al-Futuh) describe him as the horseman of 'Atlal' who crossed the Tigris under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and conquered Muqan.

full: Ja'far ibn Abi Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib b. Hashim b. 'Abd manaf b. Quasyy b. Kilab
full_name_ar: جعفر بن أبي سفيان بن الحارث ( رضي الله عنه
bio: Ibn Hajar's al-Isaba (entry 1168) quotes Ibn Sa'd that his family reported he was present at Hunayn, lived into the time of Mu'awiya and died in the middle of his reign. Ibn Shahin adds that he stayed with the Prophet together with his father until the Prophet's death. Ibn Hibban states he became Muslim with his father, witnessed Hunayn, that his mother was Hamama bint Abi Talib, and that he died in Damascus in the year 50.

full: Zinira, Roman Slave girl

bio: Wikipedia describes her as a Roman slave woman in Mecca and one of the first converts to Islam, enslaved by Banu Makhzum and Abu Jahl, who beat her after her conversion. She lost and then regained her eyesight, and was freed by Abu Bakr along with Lubaynah; she died after the Hijra, date unknown. The page cites Ibn Sa'd's Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kabir vol. 8, Ibn Ishaq's Sira and Ibn al-Athir's Usd al-Ghaba.
research_evidence: Zinira al-Rumiya (Arabic: زنيرة الرومية, Zinira the Roman) ... was a woman in Arabia, an early convert to Islam and one of the disciples (Sahaba) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
